title: DSM-103 Full Course Recap
kicker: DSM-103 Data Structures · full course recap · S01–S19 (Somnath Dey, Surya Prakash)
legend: the structure: how the data is laid out (nodes, pointers, array slots, the active element)

footer: Full-course recap for DSM-103 Data Structures, S01–S19 (Prof. Somnath Dey; Prof. Surya Prakash). Built from the lecture notes in lectures/. Every trace, index, traversal and statement count on this page was recomputed in Python and matches the lecture's worked examples. Steps that the lecture left unfinished are marked as completed by the recap: heap-sort passes 3–8, BFS steps 8–11, and the merge comparison counts. The widgets replay the lecture's own trees, heaps, graph and arrays.
course_notes: Central contrast (kept from the existing page): amber = the structure and its layout (node, pointer, array slot, the element currently being compared or moved); teal = the operation and its cost (the step taken, the finished or sorted part, the Big-O). In steppers, the active node, pair or column is amber and the visited, sorted or done part is teal. Instructors: Prof. Somnath Dey (S12–S17-18; S16 was announced as his last session, but the S17-18 sorting file is also his) and Prof. Surya Prakash (S19, and S11 earlier). There are no currency or physical units. Indices are 1-based unless a card says 0-based; show both index conventions where the lecture did (heap and array tree). Conventions the page must keep: root at level 0; height = number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path = max level + 1; max nodes = 2^h − 1. Exam-format statements in the notes: S16 says the exam will usually give an adjacency list or matrix (not a picture) and ask for a DFS or BFS from a given vertex. S19 says heap sort and quick sort are not compulsory. Assigned work: S16 asks students to run DFS and BFS on the two slide graphs; S19 asks them to show that selection sort is not stable and to solve T(n) = T(n−1) + O(n) by substitution. S13 asks students to read the LMS slides up to BST; S14 says the traversal algorithms on the slides must be studied. S12, S13, S15 and S17-18 flagged nothing for the exam. Refer back to existing modules rather than repeating them: m1 (bubble-sort passes), m5 (stacks, used by DFS), m6 (queues, used by BFS), m7 (Big-O rules).

modules.plan: Module 'Trees: vocabulary, binary-tree types and properties' (S12). Content type: derivation / framework (cards plus ONE classifier widget). Cheat cards: linear vs non-linear (a linked list is non-contiguous but still sequential; a tree is hierarchical); terminology table (node, edge/link/branch, parent = immediate predecessor, child, root (one, no parent), leaf/external node, level, height, degree/arity, siblings = same parent); course convention: root at level 0, height = max level + 1 (other textbooks differ, so use the course's); n-ary is decided by the MAXIMUM possible children, so a one-node binary tree is still binary; binary node = data + left + right; recursive tree definition (finite set of >= 1 nodes, root, disjoint subtrees T1..Tn); string form root(T1,...,Tn) with the 12-node example; binary tree recursive definition (may be EMPTY, unlike a general tree); complete / almost complete (all levels but the last full, last filled left to right) / strictly binary (0 or 2 children, leaves at any level); properties: 2^L per level, max 2^h − 1 (GP derivation), min h, E = N − 1, h = log2(n+1) complete and ceil(log2(n+1)) almost complete, n0 = n2 + 1 (edge-count proof); course plan: binary tree → BST → heap, and AVL / B-tree are not covered. Notes and analogies (cite S12): the family tree (grandparents → uncle, aunt, mother, father → cousins, brother, you) shows hierarchy, and a cousin is not a sibling; the expression tree removes the need for parentheses (operators internal, operands at leaves); 'every tree algorithm is passed only the root', like passing only the head of a linked list; the doubly linked list also has two pointers, but they mean previous/next, not left/right, and a tree grows exponentially in both directions; corrected mistakes: max is 2^h − 1 with the −1 OUTSIDE the exponent (2^(h−1) is the last level's count), and min nodes is h, not h + 1; 'leaves can be at any level; don't assume the last level'; the spoken 'n − 1' in property 5 is n + 1. Applications previewed: priority queue in O(1) via heap; BST for searching. ONE widget, 'Shape classifier': the lecture's 15-node tree numbered 1–15 level by level (SVG). Clicking a node removes or restores it; removing a node removes its subtree. Live readouts: n, height h (levels), n0 / n1 / n2, edges = n − 1, the n0 = n2 + 1 check, 2^h − 1 for this h, and ceil(log2(n+1)). Three badges: complete / almost complete / strictly binary, teal = yes and amber = no, each with a one-line reason (e.g. 'node 6 has only one child'). Presets: (1) all 15 nodes (complete + strictly binary); (2) the lecture's '13, 14, 15 missing' (almost complete, NOT strictly binary); (3) 'gap on the left of the last level': node 8 missing (neither complete nor almost complete; the lecture gave the idea, the node choice is illustrative); (4) '12 and 13 missing' (strictly binary but neither complete nor almost complete; illustrative). Worked problems: write the string form of the 12-node tree; derive 2^h − 1 by the GP sum; prove n0 = n2 + 1 and check it on the 5-leaf / 4-two-child picture.

modules.plan: Module 'Representing and traversing binary trees' (S13). Content type: algorithmic (two steppers). Cheat cards: array representation, level-wise, 1-based: LC 2i, RC 2i + 1, parent floor(i/2) (integer division); 0-based (supplementary): 2i + 1, 2i + 2, floor((i − 1)/2); array size 2^h − 1 for h levels; the right-skewed waste table; linked node LC | DATA | RC ('not literally a linked list'), space-efficient; the six orders (R TL TR = pre, TL R TR = in, TL TR R = post; the other three are reverses); recursive PREORDER / INORDER / POSTORDER pseudocode with O(n) time and O(h) stack (supplementary); in → infix, pre → prefix, post → postfix; reconstruction rules: root = first of pre / last of post, in-order gives the split, valid pairs are pre + in and post + in, not pre + post; expression trees are strictly binary (binary operators only), can be complete or almost complete. Notes and analogies (cite S13): students proposed separate odd/even parent rules and the instructor asked for one generic formula, floor(i/2) (5/2 → 2); the right-skewed tree 2 → 10 → 13 → 16 sits at 1, 3, 7, 15 and wastes 11 of 15 slots (the instructor first said h = 3, then corrected to 4); 'precedence is already built into the tree's hierarchy': higher precedence sits lower, so no brackets; converting infix to prefix by hand must respect associativity (+/− left to right: A + B − C → − + A B C; exponent right to left); traversal by hand is 'not just bottom-up then top-down': go left to a leaf, finish the whole left subtree, apply the rule in every subtree; 'one sequence alone is not enough'. TWO widgets. (a) 'Traversal stepper' (Player, pre.pcode with the three procedures; a radio button picks pre / in / post): the tree as SVG, the current call's node amber, visited nodes teal, live vars = node, call-stack depth, output string. Preset 1: the expression tree (+ (− A B) (* C (/ E F))); final readout shows the expression form (prefix / infix / postfix). Preset 2: the 15 / 10 / 20 / 8 / 12 / 16 / 25 tree with an array strip (indices 1–7) below it; the current node's i, 2i, 2i + 1 and floor(i/2) are shown live. (b) 'Rebuild from two traversals' stepper: each step takes the root from pre (first) or post (last), highlights it amber in the in-order row, colours the left and right blocks teal, and grows the tree. Preset 1 = Example 1 (pre + in of the expression tree); Preset 2 = Example 2 (in 4 8 2 5 1 6 3 7, post 8 4 5 2 6 7 3 1). Verdict at the end: the in-order and post-order of the built tree match ✓. Worked problems: write all three traversals of the expression tree; rebuild Example 2 (note 8 is the RIGHT child of 4); place the skewed tree in an array and count the blanks.

modules.plan: Module 'Binary search trees' (S14). Content type: algorithmic (ONE multi-preset stepper). Cheat cards: BST property (left subtree < node < right subtree, recursively at EVERY node); search cost O(h): O(log n) complete/balanced, O(n) skewed (table); SEARCH-BST iterative pseudocode (ptr, flag; exits on found or NULL; O(1) extra space); INSERT-BST (search to the NULL slot, track parent, attach; duplicate check); duplicates: '<' else right sends an equal key right, '<=' sends it left, and BSTs normally reject duplicates (which 28 would you delete?); sorted input → skewed (ascending → right-skewed, descending → left-skewed, random → roughly balanced); BST vs the binary search ALGORITHM (sorted array, mid = floor((low + high)/2), O(log n)); in-order of a BST is ascending, while pre/post show no order; deletion's three cases (leaf; one child; two children → in-order successor = leftmost of the right subtree, or predecessor = rightmost of the left subtree, and that node has at most one child); DELETE-BST pseudocode with the parent pointer; a BST can be rebuilt from one pre- or post-order by sorting it to get the in-order. Notes and analogies (cite S14): months as string keys, compared character by character; 'can both children be greater than the parent?' (in a general binary tree yes, in a BST no); the left-skewed chain 105, 95, 85, … gives no gain over a list, and the fix is AVL (not covered); 'for sorted data use binary search on the array instead'; the 24-becomes-ancestor-of-29 question ('only the BST property matters'); 'why not move the left child up?': it leaves a hole at every level, while the successor needs at most one easy removal; the parent pointer is needed because you unlink a node by changing its PARENT's pointer (to delete 27, set 24.right = NULL); the traversal algorithms on the slides must be studied. ONE widget, 'BST lab' (Player): SVG tree, pre.pcode switching between SEARCH-BST / INSERT-BST / DELETE-BST, live vars ptr, parent, flag, key, comparisons; the node being compared is amber and the discarded subtree is greyed (the 'halved search space'). The readout below always shows the in-order sequence, teal while sorted. Presets on the 65-tree: search 25 (4 comparisons), search 57, search 58 (fails at 57's NULL right link), insert 90 (right of 88), insert 52 (left of 57), insert duplicate 28 under '<' else right (ends as left child of 52). Preset: build from 20, 25, 27, 30, 40, 50 (right-skewed; the readout shows 'height 6 = n, search O(n)'). Presets on the 35-tree: delete 27 (leaf), delete 45 (one child → 42 moves up), delete 24 (one child → 27 becomes 29's left), delete 20 (two children → successor 24 copied up, then case 2). Verdict per deletion: which case applied and the in-order before/after. Worked problems: trace search 58; delete 20 via successor and via predecessor 16; where does a second 28 go under '<' versus '<='.

modules.plan: Module 'Heap trees, heap sort and threaded binary trees' (S15). Content type: algorithmic (ONE heap stepper) plus framework cards for threaded trees. Cheat cards: why a heap (a BST degrades on sorted input and cannot model priority); two properties: order (max-heap parent >= children, min-heap parent <= children, NO sibling order) AND shape (complete / almost complete, last level filled from the left); the root holds the max (or min); only the root is deleted (a heap can't be searched: is 35 left or right?); array representation has no gaps because of the shape property; 1-based LC 2i, RC 2i + 1, parent floor(i/2) (left children at even indices); 0-based parent floor((i − 1)/2) ONLY for 0-based; INSERT (place at the next slot, sift up vs parent); DELETE (move the last element to the root, sift down, swap with the LARGER child); costs: insert O(h) = O(log n) with at most h swaps; delete O(1) remove + O(log n) restore; HEAPSORT (swap root with the last active element, shrink, sift down; n − 1 deletions; O(n log n); in place; building from a random array first costs O(n log n) by inserts or O(n) bottom-up — supplementary); threaded binary tree: 2n links, n − 1 used, n + 1 null; LTag/RTag bits; a null left link threads to the in-order predecessor and a null right link to the successor; dummy/header node at both ends; INORDER_THREADED needs no stack (O(1) extra space). Notes and analogies (cite S15): office printer where top management's jobs print first (priority queue); free memory blocks with the largest handed out first (max-heap); min-heap when rank 1 = top priority; students guessed 'left of 55' for 120, corrected to 'left of 35' (fill the level left to right); 1000 nodes ≈ log2 1000 ≈ 10 comparisons; '111 doesn't need to check its sibling 75, which was already < 85'; deletion called 'the most important part'; the deletion constant 'into three' → O(3h) = O(h); 'you should know there is a concept of threaded binary tree'; the slide's thread arrows had copy-paste errors; B's left link cannot point to A because A is not its predecessor. ONE widget, 'Heap stepper' (Player): tree SVG and the 1-based array strip in sync; pre.pcode switches between INSERT / DELETE / HEAPSORT; live vars n, i, parent = floor(i/2) (or l, r, largest), swaps so far vs h. The compared pair is amber, the sorted tail is teal behind a '|' divider. Presets, chained in the lecture's order: insert 19 (stops at once); insert 111 (3 swaps to the root); insert 120 (3 swaps); separately, delete-root on the original 9-heap; heap sort of the original 9-heap with all 8 passes (passes 1–2 as in the lecture, 3–8 marked 'completed by the recap'). The verdict after each operation is 'heap property restored after k swaps (max h = 4)'. Threaded tree: a static card with the node layout and the thread table (no widget). Worked problems: insert 120 into the 11-node heap by hand; delete the root of the 9-heap; first two heap-sort passes; count the null links for 3 nodes (4).

modules.plan: Module 'Graphs: representation, families, DFS and BFS' (S16). Content type: framework cards (representations, terminology, families) + algorithmic (ONE traversal stepper). Cheat cards: applications table (computer, social, follow-network = directed, collaboration, information, software, road/Google Maps with one-way = directed, mobile towers, biological): 'model it as a graph and standard algorithms apply'; G = (V, E), V non-empty, E may be empty (three isolated vertices is a graph); directed vs undirected; simple / multigraph (multiplicity m, no loops) / loop / pseudograph; adjacency list (order inside a list implies NOTHING about edges among those nodes; symmetric if undirected); adjacency matrix (symmetric if undirected, store half; multiplicity counts; a loop puts a nonzero value on the diagonal); incidence matrix (vertices × edges, two 1s per column, row sum = degree, edge identity readable); degree-reading table (matrix: out = row sum, in = column sum; list: out = list length, in = scan every list, costly at 1000 vertices; so prefer a matrix if you need in-degree often); edge counts (undirected ½ΣM, directed ΣM, incidence ½Σ = number of columns); K_n, C_n (n >= 3), Q_n (2^n vertices, adjacent iff the labels differ in one bit), bipartite (the class example V1 = {A, B, D}, V2 = {C, E, F, G}); DFS = stack (go deep, backtrack), BFS = queue (level by level); the pseudocode for both; traversals are not unique; reference complexities O(V + E) list / O(V^2) matrix (not stated in lecture); MST and shortest paths are deferred to the Algorithms course. Notes and analogies (cite S16): 'A follows B, B need not follow A'; one-way roads as directed edges; 'if A's list is B → C → E that does not mean B and C are connected'; the lecturer misspoke 'DFS uses queue' and corrected it to stack; 'write the output with commas, not arrows: A → B → D does not mean an edge B–D'; popping stale duplicates IS the backtracking; the exam gives an adjacency list or matrix, not the picture; assigned: finish DFS and BFS on the two slide graphs; 'come with specific, solid points' for doubt sessions; Prof. Surya takes over. ONE widget, 'DFS / BFS stepper' (Player) on the 7-vertex graph: SVG graph (E as the hub, the F-G-C triangle), a toggle DFS / BFS, pre.pcode of the chosen algorithm with the line highlighted, and a container strip (stack drawn with the top at the RIGHT; queue drawn front → rear) where pushed entries appear and stale entries are struck through when discarded. Live vars v, visited set, output. The current vertex is amber, visited vertices are teal, and the tree edge used is highlighted. It replays the lecture's push/enqueue orders exactly (A pushes B, D, E; E pushes D, B, C, F; …). Final readouts: DFS A, E, F, G, C, B, D; BFS A, B, D, E, C, F, G with levels 0/1/2/3 drawn as bands. A third preset 'reversed neighbour order (computed, not from lecture)' gives DFS A, B, C, E, D, F, G, to show non-uniqueness. Worked problems: degrees and edge count from the 4-vertex adjacency matrix; is 001 adjacent to 011 / 010 in Q3; the DFS trace from A.
modules.facts: Traversal graph edges (reconstructed): AB, AD, AE, BC, BE, DE, CE, EF, FC, FG, GC → |E| = 11; degrees A3 B3 C4 D2 E5 F3 G2, sum 22 = 2·11 (handshaking, not covered). DFS stack after each visit: A → [B D E]; E → [B D D B C F]; F → [B D D B C C G]; G → [B D D B C C C]; C → [B D D B C C] (pushes nothing new); discard C, C; B visited → [B D D]; D visited → [B D]; discard D, B → output A, E, F, G, C, B, D. BFS queue: A → [B D E]; B → [D E E C]; D → [E E C E]; E → [E C E C F]; skip E; C → [E C F G]; skip E, C; F; G → output A, B, D, E, C, F, G (lecture stopped at A, B, D, E, C; steps 8–11 completed by the note); levels 0: A; 1: B, D, E; 2: C, F; 3: G. Directed example: A has 3 incident edges, 2 out and 1 in. Multigraph: 3 parallel A–B edges → M[A][B] = 3. modules.plan: Module 'Sorting I: improved bubble sort, selection sort, in-place' (S17-18, a double session). Content type: algorithmic + numerical. Bubble-sort passes are already in m1: refer back and do NOT re-teach the [7, 2, 9, 6, 4] pass table; add only what is new. Cheat cards: sorting definition; comparison-based (bubble, selection, insertion, quick, merge, heap, shell) vs non-comparison (bucket, counting, radix); bubble guarantee: after one pass the LARGEST is at the end, the smallest is NOT guaranteed at the front; n − 1 passes; version 1 loop bounds (0-indexed j = 0..n − i − 2) and version 2 (1-indexed j = 1..n − i, with the swapped flag → early break); statement count T(n) = Σ[3(n − i) + 2] = 1.5n^2 + 0.5n − 2 → O(n^2); best case (sorted) 3n − 3 → O(n), worst (smallest at the end) O(n^2), average O(n^2); in-place = constant auxiliary space independent of n (even 100 variables), with the temp-variable swap; selection sort: sorted | unsorted partition, find the min INDEX, swap it to the front, at most one swap per pass, 'if min != i'; T(n) = Σ[2(n − i) + 2] = n^2 + n − 2, or n^2 + 3n − 4 if the swap counts as 3 statements ('constants don't matter'); selection has no sortedness check, so its best case is O(n^2); comparison table (best O(n) vs O(n^2), worst and average both O(n^2), both in-place). Notes and analogies (cite S17-18): 'bubble' = the largest rises like a bubble from the bottom of a pond, and 'sinking' = in descending order the smallest sinks to the bottom; a student said 2 and 9 were sorted after pass 1 and the lecturer replied that 2 reaching the front was a coincidence; bubble sort is 'mainly a teaching algorithm'; comparisons are about equal, but bubble swaps on every out-of-order pair while selection swaps once per pass, so 'if you must choose, choose selection sort'; the min-index walkthrough (min moves to position 4 at value 10, then to position 7 at value 8). ONE widget, 'Bubble vs selection, side by side' (Player): two array strips and two pre.pcode panels (improved bubble; selection) stepping in lockstep, one comparison per step. Live vars: bubble i, j, swapped; selection i, j, min. Counters: comparisons and swaps for each algorithm. The compared pair or current min is amber and the sorted region teal (the tail for bubble, the front for selection). Presets: [7, 2, 9, 6, 4] (the lecture's array; bubble 10 comparisons / 6 swaps vs selection 10 / 4); [2, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13] (the lecture's already-sorted example: bubble breaks after one pass with 5 comparisons, selection still does 15). The verdict line names the winner on swaps, or on comparisons for sorted input. A static card table gives the statement counts for n = 5, 10, 100 (no chart). Worked problems: derive 1.5n^2 + 0.5n − 2; derive n^2 + n − 2 and the 3-statement-swap variant; selection sort on [7, 2, 9, 6, 4] by hand.

modules.plan: Module 'Merge sort, stability and recurrences' (S19, Prof. Surya Prakash). Content type: algorithmic (merge stepper) + derivation (recurrence cards) + a small case widget for stability. Cheat cards: sorting output = a permutation with a'1 <= … <= a'n; internal (all in RAM) vs external (part on disk); in-place = O(1) extra; stable = equal keys keep their input order; stability table (bubble, merge, insertion, counting stable; selection, heap, quick NOT stable; heap and quick not compulsory); divide → conquer → combine with the P / P1 / P11 / S11 problem tree; recursion = a method calling itself on a different range (hence the p, r parameters); MERGE-SORT(A, p, r) with q = floor((p + r)/2), initial call (A, 1, n); MERGE(A, p, q, r): n1 = q − p + 1, n2 = r − q, copy into L and R, pointers i, j, fill A[k]; use L[i] <= R[j] for stability (the lecturer said '<'); leftover handling: copy the remainder, or use ∞ sentinels; MERGE is O(N) time and O(n) space, so merge sort is NOT in-place; recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), T(1) = a; substitution with n = 2^k: T(n) = 2^k T(n/2^k) + kcn + (2^k − 1)c0 → an + cn log2 n + (n − 1)c0 = O(n log n); summary table. Notes and analogies (cite S19): student records A 80, B 70, C 80, D 60, where an unstable sort could 'unfairly push back someone who was ahead'; 'one comparison per output element because both fronts are the only candidates for the minimum', versus unsorted lists needing O(n^2); padding a non-power of 2 (e.g. 17) with dummy elements; method1 → method2 → method3 versus a method calling itself; the lecturer said 'ceiling' and corrected it to floor (floor 4.5 = 4); the last term is 'some constant', strictly (n − 1)c0. Assigned: show that selection sort is not stable; solve T(n) = T(n − 1) + O(n). Next session: searching. TWO widgets. (a) 'Merge-sort tree' (Player): the 7-element input split top-down level by level (amber = the range being divided, with p, q, r shown), then merged bottom-up; during each merge, pre.pcode MERGE is highlighted with live L, R, i, j, k and the two fronts compared in amber, while finished runs turn teal. Per-merge comparison counter (copy-remainder version). Presets: [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10] (the lecture's example) and [2, 8, 3, 7, 3, 9, 3] with the three 3s tagged 3a / 3b / 3c, so the stable output order 3a, 3b, 3c is visible. (b) 'Stable or not?' (case widget): the lecture's records A 80, B 70, C 80, D 60 with buttons 'merge sort' and 'selection sort'. It shows the output order with A and C coloured; the verdict reads 'stable: A stays ahead of C' or 'unstable: C jumped ahead of A (the long-distance swap of A with D at pass 1)'. Worked problems: merge [27, 38] + [3, 43] step by step; the substitution derivation to O(n log n); the assigned T(n) = T(n − 1) + cn → O(n^2).
modules.facts: Sorting example: 8, 2, 4, 9, 3, 6 → 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9. Stability examples: 2, 5, 8, 5, 3 → 2, 3, 5, 5, 8; 2, 8, 3, 7, 3, 9, 3 → 2, 3, 3, 3, 7, 8, 9. Merge input (reconstructed) [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10]: MERGE-SORT(A, 1, 7) q = floor(8/2) = 4 → [38, 27, 43, 3] | [9, 82, 10]; (5, 7) q = floor(12/2) = 6 → [9, 82] | [10]; merges: [27, 38], [3, 43], [9, 82], [10]; [3, 27, 38, 43]; [9, 10, 82]; final [3, 9, 10, 27, 38, 43, 82]. Merge [27, 38] + [3, 43]: 27 vs 3 → 3; 27 vs 43 → 27; 38 vs 43 → 38; copy 43 → 3 comparisons. Computed comparison counts (copy-remainder): 1 + 1 + 1 + 3 + 2 + 6 = 14. 8-element call: q = floor((1 + 8)/2) = floor(4.5) = 4 → (1, 4), (5, 8), MERGE(A, 1, 4, 8). n1 = q − p + 1, n2 = r − (q + 1) + 1 = r − q; indices 1..6 → 6 − 1 + 1 = 6. Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn + c0; after k steps 2^k T(n/2^k) + kcn + (2^k − 1)c0; k = log2 n → an + cn log2 n + (n − 1)c0; e.g. n = 8, k = 3: 8a + 24c + 7c0. Assigned: T(n) = T(n − 1) + cn → c(n + (n − 1) + … + 2) + a = c(n(n + 1)/2 − 1) + a = O(n^2). Computed selection sort on records (ascending by marks, strict <): i=1 min D60 swap with A80 → D60, B70, C80, A80; i=2 B70 stays; i=3 A80 not < C80 → no swap → D60, B70, C80, A80 (C ahead of A: unstable). Merge sort (<=) → D60, B70, A80, C80. Computed: selection sort happens to keep 3a, 3b, 3c in order on 2, 8, 3, 7, 3, 9, 3, so it is not a counter-example.
